title: 2. Bundesliga: Zivzivadze header earns Heidenheim narrow win at Fürth
description: 1. FC Heidenheim secured their third victory of the 2026/27 2. Bundesliga campaign with a hard-fought 1-0 win away to Greuther Fürth on Sunday.Budu Zivzivadze’s first-half header was enough to sepa...
fullText:
1. FC Heidenheim secured their third victory of the 2026/27 2. Bundesliga campaign with a hard-fought 1-0 win away to Greuther Fürth on Sunday.

Budu Zivzivadze's first-half header was enough to separate the two sides, with Frank Schmidt's side showing impressive defensive resilience to preserve their lead despite Fürth controlling large periods of the contest.

The result sees Heidenheim move into the top three after four matches, while Fürth suffer their second defeat of the season.

The hosts started brightly and almost opened the scoring inside the opening 10 minutes.

Felix Klaus found space inside the Heidenheim penalty area before getting a shot away, but his effort was unable to beat goalkeeper Thomas Dähne.

Heidenheim soon demonstrated why they have been among the division's more dangerous sides in attack, however, and they took the lead with their first major opportunity.

In the 12th minute, Marcel Costly delivered an inviting cross into the Fürth penalty area. Zivzivadze rose highest and directed a powerful header beyond Florian Hellstern to put the visitors 1-0 ahead.

The goal forced Fürth to chase the game, with the hosts continuing to see more of the ball and looking to find a route through Heidenheim's compact defensive structure.

Felix Klaus remained a constant threat, while Luca Itter came particularly close to an equaliser in the 32nd minute. The Fürth defender found space in a dangerous position but could not find a way past Dähne.

Heidenheim, meanwhile, were content to defend deep and look for opportunities on the counterattack.

The visitors went into the break with their narrow advantage intact, despite Fürth arguably having enjoyed the better of the opening 45 minutes.

Heidenheim almost doubled their lead not long after the restart. Alessandro Vogt found himself in a promising position in the 50th minute, but he was unable to beat Hellstern and put the game beyond Fürth.

Just five minutes later, Oualid Mhamdi was presented with another opportunity as Heidenheim looked to exploit the space left by an increasingly attacking Fürth side. However, the visitors again failed to find the decisive second goal.

Fürth continued to dominate possession as the half progressed, but Heiko Vogel's side struggled to turn their territorial advantage into clear-cut opportunities.

The hosts introduced Jordan Siebatcheu and Omar Sillah during the closing stages in an attempt to inject fresh attacking impetus into the game.

Despite the changes, Fürth were unable to seriously threaten Dähne's goal.

Heidenheim's defensive organisation remained impressive as the visitors protected their lead, with their back line repeatedly dealing with Fürth's crosses and attacking moves.

The final stages saw Fürth continue to push forward in search of an equaliser, but their finishing ultimately let them down.

Heidenheim survived the pressure and secured a valuable clean sheet, with the 1-0 victory marking their first shutout of the campaign.

The result represents another positive step for Heidenheim following their relegation from the Bundesliga last season. Three wins from their opening four league matches have put Schmidt's side firmly among the early promotion contenders.

For Fürth, meanwhile, the defeat leaves them with four points from their opening four matches. Despite producing some of the more attractive football during Sunday's encounter, the hosts were ultimately punished for failing to make their opportunities count.

title: What Utah Tech coach Lance Anderson said after losing to BYU
description: Upon falling 63-7 to BYU Saturday night in Provo, Utah Tech head coach Lance Anderson has a better understanding of why so many people have projected the Cougars to be a potential College Football Playoff squad.  With the loss, Utah Tech falls to 0-2 on the season, having been defeated 54-0 by defending FCS national champion Montana State this past week.
fullText:
Upon falling 63-7 to BYU Saturday night in Provo, Utah Tech head coach Lance Anderson has a better understanding of why so many people have projected the Cougars to be a potential College Football Playoff squad.

"Obviously it's hard to say after one game, and obviously we did not match up real well with them, but you look at their roster and I think they got a lot of those (championship caliber) pieces," Anderson told reporters postgame.

"Especially if some of these young receivers continue to come through, because I think it starts with the quarterback. You've got an outstanding running back in L.J. Martin ... great kid. They're physical up front on both sides of the ball, offensive line, defensive line. I think they've got some very athletic players in that linebacker room and DB room. So I think they've got the pieces in place. I think it'll be interesting to see how the year plays out."

Anderson, a longtime Stanford assistant, knows BYU's Kalani Sitake well, having faced off both in the Pac-12 and FCS ranks prior to Saturday. Anderson's daughter even worked for Sitake during her schooling at BYU.

"I think what's made him so successful is he understands BYU well," Anderson said of Sitake. "Being here as a player, being here as a coach, I think he understands this place and what it's about and what it represents. He's done a great job of building this (program), I think he's done it his way with his personality. That, I think, leads to that sustained and long-term success."

Anderson is also well-acquainted with new Cougars defensive coordinator Kelly Poppinga, whose starters impressed on Saturday before the backups surrendered a lone fourth quarter touchdown.

"I think he's an outstanding football coach," Anderson said of Poppinga. "You look at the film from last year, the last couple years with Jay Hill as a defensive coordinator, I think they've got a very good system and they've not really strayed far from that. We could see that tonight, but I think Kelly's brought a few wrinkles of his own from his time with Bronco Mendenhall and his coaching experience. I think he'll do a phenomenal job as a defensive coordinator.

"... I think BYU's got a great team, and I think they're going to be very successful this year."

With the loss, Utah Tech falls to 0-2 on the season, having been defeated 54-0 by defending FCS national champion Montana State this past week.

Anderson's Trailblazers, picked to finish last in the Big Sky Conference, will continue their early gauntlet in visiting heavily-favored Montana next week.

"I think games like this are fun opportunities," Anderson said. "Opening the season against the No. 1 FCS team in the country, Montana State, that's a great challenge. Being able to play in this environment at BYU today, great, great opportunity.

"We get a chance to go to Montana next week, which is another tremendous place to play, where that place is gonna be packed, it's gonna be loud. Fans are right on top of you. So our guys are excited about this, they're gonna go out and compete."

title: Sheffield United 1-3 Norwich City: Canaries Hand Blades First Defeat of Campaign
description: Sheffield United suffered a 3-1 home defeat against Norwich City on Saturday afternoon, marking the first loss of the campaign for the Blades.The visitors took the lead inside the opening ten minutes ...
fullText:
Sheffield United suffered a 3-1 home defeat against Norwich City on Saturday afternoon, marking the first loss of the campaign for the Blades.

The visitors took the lead inside the opening ten minutes when former Owls man Anthony Musaba found the back of the net. United equalised soon after with an emphatic finish from Patrick Bamford. However, the Canaries managed to find another goal just before half-time through Mohamed Toure. Shortly after the hour mark, Mathias Kvistgaarden delivered the final blow after a goalmouth scramble in front of the away end.

Blades: Cooper, Tanganga, Choudhury, Donovan (Arblaster 77), Kitching, Brereton Diaz (Shackleton 77), Campbell (Cannon 58), Norrington-Davies (McCallum 58), Peck, Riedewald (Phillips 45), Bamford.

Unused: Davies, Rothwell, McGuinness, Baptiste.

Norwich: Kovacevic, Mattsson, Brooks (Crnac 85), Chrisene, McConville (Darling 85), Slimane (Wright 61), Toure (Kvistgaarden 61), McLean, Córdoba, Fisher, Musaba (Diallo 70).

Unused: Grimshaw, Stacey, Yongwa, Maghoma.

Neither side had done enough to establish control during the opening stages, but Norwich needed just one real opportunity to break the deadlock.

The visitors patiently shifted possession across the edge of the United penalty area before Brooks and Pelle Mattsson combined to create the opening. The ball was worked into the path of Musaba, who made no mistake, curling a right-footed finish into the top corner beyond Michael Cooper.

Brooks, making his return to Bramall Lane, almost added to Norwich's advantage soon afterwards. The former Blades man connected with a McLean corner but could only send his volley beyond the far post.

United responded and began to threaten at the other end.

Sydie Peck found space down the left channel on 17 minutes and unleashed a powerful effort, but Norwich goalkeeper Vladan Kovacevic stood firm to keep it out.

From the resulting corner, Liam Kitching appeared to have levelled when he rose highest at the far post and headed into the net. However, the goal was ruled out after the referee spotted a foul on Kovacevic.

The Blades did not have to wait much longer for their equaliser. On 23 minutes, Campbell helped create the opening, with Brereton Diaz's ball finding Patrick Bamford in a promising position. United's number 45 showed his quality, producing a composed left-footed finish to restore parity.

With the game finely balanced, both teams looked capable of taking control, but Norwich struck again just before the interval. A flick from former Blade Slimane sent the ball into the path of Toure, who broke away from the United defence before calmly finding the back of the net. The forward was subsequently booked for his celebrations as Norwich headed into the break with a 2-1 advantage.

Chris Wilder's side needed a response after the restart and substitute Kalvin Phillips almost provided it with a spectacular effort. The midfielder unleashed a fierce strike from around 30 yards, only to see the attempt narrowly miss the post.

United continued to search for another route back into the game, but Norwich delivered the decisive blow through another player introduced from the bench. Kvistgaarden had barely been on the pitch when he reacted quickest to a loose ball and fired home to give the visitors a two-goal cushion.

There was still time for the Blades to mount a late comeback. Bamford tried to force his way into a dangerous position late on, but Chrisene made an important challenge to halt his progress.

United continued pushing in the closing stages, with Sam McCallum sending an effort over the crossbar deep into added time.

Sheffield United are back in action in midweek when they travel to Lancashire to take on Blackburn Rovers.

Sulaiman and Kasim Khan slammed PCB chief Mohsin Naqvi for threatening to boycott the Lord's Test over an interview about Imran Khan.

Imran's sons called the board's attempt to censor the broadcast "tactless" and said officials made "absolute fools of themselves".

The political interference adds to the ongoing crisis in Pakistan cricket, where off-field drama continues to eclipse Test match performances.

The chaos surrounding the PCB has reached political farce, with former captain Imran Khan's sons publicly roasting PCB Chairman Mohsin Naqvi for threatening to boycott the Lord's Test. Reports emerged during the second Test that Naqvi, who also serves as Pakistan's Interior Minister, threw a fit over a Sky Sports feature where Michael Atherton interviewed Imran's sons regarding their father's health in prison.

In a desperate attempt to censor the broadcast, board officials allegedly threatened to pull the national team off the field entirely. While captain Babar Azam and former head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed scrambled to deny knowledge of a strike, the public damage was already done.

Rather than managing a high-performance cricket setup, Naqvi's board has used the national team as a political instrument on foreign soil, exposing the PCB's complete lack of professional governance.

MORE: 'Victory vs India …..': Mohammad Yousuf reveals what led to Pakistan cricket's downfall

It shouldn't be in the remit of the Pakistan Cricket Board to ask for an interview about an ex-Pakistan player, somebody who lived in England for 22 years, to be taken down. While the PCB busies itself seizing players' phones and censoring TV broadcasts, the national team continues to suffer embarrassing defeats on the pitch. Naqvi's tenure as PCB chairman has turned a proud cricket nation into a geopolitical laughingstock.

Until political appointees are stripped of their power and replaced by genuine administrators, Pakistan cricket will remain trapped in a self-inflicted nightmare where political ego always trumps athletic performance.

title: Drake Maye’s selfless approach could define Year 3 with Patriots
description: Drake Maye was asked about a Year 3 leap, and his answer said everything you need to know about the star quarterback.
fullText:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. – During his rookie season, Drake Maye certainly impressed. But it was his second season in the league when he truly emerged as one of the top quarterbacks in the league, finishing the year by leading the New England Patriots to the Super Bowl and being the MVP runner-up.

He put the league on notice, and now, going into his third year, many expect him to be even better. But has he put any thought into a potential Year 3 leap?

"Yeah, I am maybe not really focused on that, hoping we win some games," he told reporters on Saturday. "I think the more that I can, myself, put the offense into good plays and make plays and score plays with how much confidence I have in our defense, I think we will be on the right side of a lot of games.

"So, I think more Year 3 leap and Year 2 leap, I am focused on leaping each and every day and trying to get better," he added. "How can I get better? And the more you get better each and every day, I feel like whatever you guys call a leap, whatever happens, happens. So I think trying to trump 14 games last year, 14 and 3, that would be a big leap for us. So that's, that would be a challenge. And I think we got to attack it one week at a time."

The quarterback demonstrated what a true leader he is, making it clear that he was only concerned with team victories instead of personal accomplishments.

"I am looking for our team to make a leap, really instead of me," he stated.

title: How Williamsburg Lost Its Swag (2026)
description: Williamsburg’s gentrifiers are being gentrified.
fullText:
There is a place in New York City that many insist does not exist. It is primarily composed of concrete streets, old family-run stores, and a massive influx of newer, sleeker businesses with scrawled cursive logos and $7 drinks. It is called “East Willliamsburg.”

East Williamsburg, depending on who you ask, could be anything. Its geographical boundaries are contentious and ever-debated, since it has not been historically defined by government agencies, and there are no official neighborhood lines drawn, but the name has been used vaguely to refer to an industrial area of Williamsburg that developers have been trying to revitalize since at least the 1980s. For longtime residents, the neighborhood itself is about as real as Santa Claus, or the tooth fairy—“East Williamsburg” could’ve just as easily been “South Greenpoint” or “West Bushwick” or “Tatooine” or “Six Flags.” But for many, especially people who have just landed in Brooklyn, it is a very real place. More specifically, it’s a playground. East Williamsburg is a sprawling obstacle course of shops and bars, all catering to the younger new residents who have moved to New York City in order to work hard and play harder.

I have heard from haggard, decrepit millennials that it used to be different, that it used to be grungy and alternative. That’s not the Williamsburg I know. I know a Williamsburg where there’s not just one, but two Whole Foods, and one of them is a combination building with a Capital One bank. Gwyneth Paltrow is allegedly opening a Goop store, too. I know it as the “most exciting Asian American coffee hotspot,” which is a title that I feel represents both a very cool thing happening for sprouting businesses and sometimes also the fourth horseman of the apocalypse. While the neighborhood used to be renowned for flannel-clad IPA connoisseurs and a thriving indie art scene, the 2010s-era hipsters who sparked the Hasidim vs. Hipsters war have now been usurped by a new stereotype: the tech bro.

It wasn’t always this way. For decades, the wider area of Williamsburg has held a major cultural fascination for the type of millennial transplant who makes their way out to the East Coast. Williamsburg is the setting for the 2010s CBS sitcom 2 Broke Girls, the story of how a billionaire’s daughter had to flee to Brooklyn after losing all her money and start over again in a diner. It’s where Dakota Johnson apparently lives while going through her post-college identity crisis in the 2010s breakup movie How to Be Single. Williamsburg is the secret fourth girl in Lena Dunham’s HBO show Girls, so consistently featured on screen that there are Sex in the City–style crawls of all the North Brooklyn businesses that appear in the show. Former Teen Vogue editor-in-chief Elaine Welteroth wrote, about moving to the newly minted East Williamsburg to chase her big magazine dreams in her memoir More Than Enough, that “to the uninitiated, this particular block in Bushwick looked mad suspect.” During this time, the archetype of who was gentrifying Williamsburg was very clear: They were cool, they were broke, they were all mentally going through something, but they were having fun, and that’s what made it all so exciting.

But in recent years, that identity has been fractured entirely. Between 2010 and 2026, rent prices have doubled in the neighborhood, and there seems to be no slowing down. According to data from Apartments.com, the average rent price in New York City is $4,197, and Williamsburg even surpasses that—the median rent price is $5,100, according to competitor platform StreetEasy. Most of the rent increases happened post-COVID. The biggest jump in recent years happened just after lockdown, beginning in May 2021, one month after all adults became eligible for vaccines nationwide.

Part of this has to do with the fact that tech companies, specifically A.I. startups, have begun settling in the area. Amazon Music and A.I.-focused ecommerce startups Queen One and Autonomous Technologies all set up shop at a Williamsburg waterfront building with floor-to-ceiling glass windows. So did A.I. software firm Rillavoice, and Altana AI, which has a two-year contract with the U.S. Customs and Border Patrol to enforce tariffs (a job that is definitely not evil and sounds super awesome). The landmark Domino Sugar factory was gut-renovated and now serves as offices for over 30 A.I. and tech firms.

If the original-format gentrification was all about moving into a neighborhood with cheap rent, this second-wave gentrification is about moving in on taste. Sure, the desire to relentlessly pursue the New Cool has always been a thing—it’s why rich people acted as benefactors for artists in exchange for party invitations and clout—but in an algorithm-dominated world, the desire to feel unique is more acute (and quantifiably rewarded in likes and reposts) than ever. It’s even become a stereotype online, the guy who works at an A.I. defense startup, reads leftist literature, is really intense about Japanese dining customs, and laments the destruction of interpersonal interactions in our modern digital age. The currency is taste: Williamsburg effectively costs the same as Manhattan prices, but there is a thrill in living in a space that has been so famously known for hosting so many interesting people before.

Williamsburg feels more bland, and it is. Tech bros are moving in, which means the area’s cultural identity is different now. This corner of Brooklyn is moving on to the next wave of gentrification: They’re culturally gentrifying the original gentrifiers, erasing the identity of precariously employed DJs who are experimenting with polyamory and microbangs. One street has become the neighborhood’s unofficial wellness avenue, where there’s just store after store of red-light therapy, bathhouses, and microneedling. Perpendicular to that, there’s a lunchtime slop-bowl corridor, offering Just Salad, Dig, Cava, and Sweetgreen in one neat little row.

But just as original-format gentrification pushes out the original community that lived there, the second wave pushes out anyone who brought swag to the table. All the handlebar mustache freaks with a Moleskine notebook and a dream have been forced to move to farther neighborhoods like Bushwick and Ridgewood, which are already skyrocketing in price, and after that, they’ll probably have to extend the train farther into the no-man’s land of Middle Village or make up another new neighborhood or something. In turn, Williamsburg has been sapped of all its affordability, and increasingly, its cool factor. Art is made when there is space to make it, and if people are under pressure to pay an average $5,100 in rent, then there’s no space for ideas to make their way to the surface. There is only space to optimize, and streamline, and organize. I walk down the street and I see an alarming number of people wearing weighted walking vests now, which is so frightening that it requires me to catch my breath every now and again. There is nothing very cool about everything becoming the same.

This isn’t the only place in the country undergoing this cultural homogenization, either. Gawker asked its readers in 2011, “What’s the Williamsburg of your city?,” which touched on the core truth—everywhere, there are hip neighborhoods that are controversial because they are started by people who are causing adverse ripple effects just because they are moving somewhere new, but they also bring hipness, an idiosyncrasy that feels like a far better trade after everything’s already been beaten into conformity. In the age of social media trends, there are plenty of cities across the country that have all wound up kind of looking the same—venture capital–backed coffee shops, LED-lit workout classes, a crowded Trader Joe’s, upscale brands that hold a certain cachet among young six-figure earners for their status products and carefully curated typefaces (Diptyque, Aesop, Le Labo, Necessaire, you get the idea). What used to set Williamsburg apart from the rest was the distinctive identity of who lived there. Now, it could be anywhere.

The millennials’ Williamsburg was not perfect, but at least it was special, and in this era of tech bros sitting at the helm of the neighborhood, it risks losing all swag entirely. Perhaps, just like in the food chain, there will be another bigger predator that takes over the city, a secret third thing that turns this generic Roblox neighborhood into something even more unrecognizable. Maybe they’ll make up more names to slice up the neighborhood, and open even more Whole Foods locations. Maybe Gwyneth Paltrow will launch the Goop store and shift the tectonic plates. But none of it will be cool. Most certainly not.

title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
description: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa decides this week whether to ban Russian-language content in music and literature in public.
fullText:
Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.

The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation.

It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.

For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.

The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.

In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions.

The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently.

"The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that," says Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on an official programme to "decolonise" the city of its historic Russian legacy.

"With Russian-speaking music and other things, Russians try to deconstruct Ukrainian identity and influence especially young people, because they grow up in a Russian-speaking environment."

But comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, says: "Russian isn't [only] the language of Putin, it's the language of [writers like] Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov.

"Who benefits from setting people against other people who love Ukraine just as deeply, only love it in a different language? Only Putin benefits from this."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has often referred to what he falsely describes as repression of the Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of his justifications for launching his invasion of the country.

Russian and Ukrainian are closely related, but distinct in many ways. Many in Ukraine speak a mixture of the two, known as surzhyk.

Russian is the native language of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which he used often in his election campaign but has since used only Ukrainian in public.

But a 2019 law requires use of Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts including education, public services and customer service.

Public-facing workers - including waiters, shop assistants and doctors - must address customers or patients initially in Ukrainian, though they can later switch to Russian if the client prefers that.

Odesa's Mask Theatre, run by Barsky, has been fined for infringements of the legislation including using Russian in publicity materials. A later inspection found further violations such as a cafe sign with the Russian word for coffee.

"This isn't even like Orwell or Kafka, it's just madness," he says.

Barsky has been able to continue to perform in Russian because it is a private theatre.

The new language proposal - similar to one already in force in the capital Kyiv and some other cities – would urge but not require private premises including shops and cafes to adopt the ban.

Odesa's state-appointed language ombudswoman, Anna Nerush, who inspects premises to check on alleged violations of the rules, thinks if passed it will put pressure on them to comply.

"All businesses interact in one way or another with local government," she told the BBC. "They rent premises, they need advertising permits, and so on. So for many entities it's important to comply with a council decision, even if doesn't provide for sanctions for non-compliance. "

Public playing of songs by Russian citizens is already illegal across Ukraine, with exceptions for some artists who have publicly condemned the war, but Russian-language songs composed or performed by Ukrainians are still allowed.

Under the proposals they would also be banned in public places.

Anna Nerush said it would not affect someone celebrating their birthday in Russian in a private room in a restaurant, as it could not be heard outside.

"But on the streets, [hearing] the Russian language can be a real trigger, for example to [former] prisoners of war and people who've come from occupied territories," she said.

Many native Russian-speakers in Ukraine have switched to Ukrainian in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

These include landmarks such as a Cossack cemetery that dates back to before 1794. That is the year Russian empress Catherine the Great is said to have founded the city, although it has been widely questioned in recent years.

A statue of Catherine was removed from a central Odesa square after a council vote in 2022, and streets have been renamed to commemorate some Ukrainian writers and activists.

"We must understand we were a colony," said Mykhailenko. "And these [language] laws are very important. I understand it's maybe sometimes not democratic. But without it, there will be no normal Ukraine in the future."

Anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky, part of a group called Ukrainian Cosmopolis which aims to defend freedom of thought and speech, believes Russian-speakers are being made to feel like second-class citizens who are deprived of their heritage.

"In Ukraine, the vast majority of people understand both Russian and Ukrainian. So the question is not really one of language, it's one of liberty," she said.

"Ukraine has been fighting for freedom. The point of this war is not to be under authoritarian rule. That's what Russia has to offer. So when fines, or the threat of being fired [for breaking language laws] arrives, then people start wondering: what are we fighting for?"

It is unclear how much support the new language proposal has. It is opposed by an influential group of councillors linked to former mayor Hennadiy Trukhanov.

Beyond Odesa, a national poll showed 80% support for Ukrainian dominating "all spheres of communication" in 2022. However, a more recent survey of students in Kyiv found that 82% chose to speak Russian during break times, even though Ukrainian is enforced in classrooms.

One famous Odesan who found himself at the centre of the language controversy is Pavlo Viktor, a physics teacher whose online lessons have been followed by millions around the world.

Ukrainian language campaigners criticised him for putting the videos out in Russian, his first language, although he later translated them into Ukrainian. He was later criticised for saying he would talk to scared children in Russian during missile attacks, if that was the language they preferred.

Viktor is keen to take the heat out of the argument, explaining that currently about 10% of the Odesa population spoke Ukrainian in the street: "But if we wait 50 years, maybe 90% will speak Ukrainian."

"Ukrainianisation must be polite and soft… not to persuade children to move from Russian to Ukrainian, but to make an atmosphere when they want to do this. It's the best way. And I hope that gradually we'll move in that direction."

You can hear more about the language controversy in Odesa in the Crossing Continents podcast Ukraine: Fighting Russia, Fighting Russian, available from Tuesday 8 September.

title: New York City pausing some AI tools in schools
description: New York City imposes a one-year moratorium on student-facing AI tools for grades K-8, citing concerns about youth mental health.
fullText:
“A six-year-old child is too young to slice an onion, to fry an egg or to use a stove safely. But once that child becomes 16, that knowledge becomes something they are mature enough to learn,” stressed New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani, while announcing a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students.

In what has been described as one of “the most expansive student-facing AI policies in the country”, the Mayor and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels on September 2 imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for pupils up to eighth grade for the 2026–27 academic year.

Here’s what you need to know about the moratorium, why NYC introduced it, and why the move could set a global precedent.

This move will affect nearly 6,00,000 public school students across the United States’ largest school district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, while the AI components of more than 38 previously approved programmes that fail to meet the new standards will be disabled or discontinued.

However, not all AI has been banned. Teachers can continue to use approved tools for planning and administrative work. Assistive technologies required by students with disabilities, as well as certain AI tools used in career-readiness programmes, remain permitted where necessary and under the policy’s safeguards.

Five limited AI pilots will also operate throughout the year for high school classrooms. These select tools are Quill (15 minutes per week) for English language arts; Edia (20 minutes per week) for mathematics; Brisk Teaching (10 to 20 minutes once or twice weekly) for teacher-created activities; Playlab (two assignments per marking period; 45 minutes per week) for assignment-specific applications; and Intel AI-Ready Schools (one period per week) to assist students in identifying community issues and developing solutions through term-long projects.

Every high school student will complete two 45-minute modules per year aimed at developing critical thinking around AI use, including its risks, limitations, and scope. Alongside AI restrictions, tighter individual screen-time limits have also been introduced. Children from 2-K through to second grade will have no routine screen time. For those in grades three to five, NYC Public Schools recommends no more than 30 minutes a day of individual screen use; for grades six to eight, the recommendation is 45 minutes. These restrictions do not prohibit teacher-led use of computers, tablets, or interactive whiteboards during lessons.

Throughout the academic year, a panel comprising students, educators, parents, elected officials, union partners, and field experts will assess the impact of the moratorium and pilots, delivering a report with policy recommendations in April 2027.

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow,” Mr. Mamdani said. “They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators, and wrestle with tough problems on their own.” Mr. Samuels also made a similar argument. Learning, he said, involves getting something wrong, trying again and eventually getting it right. That struggle is not an inconvenience that technology should eliminate; it is part of the learning process.

This move arrives amidst growing concern over screen time harming youth mental health. Studies have linked excessive scrolling, social media exposure and reliance on AI in children to lower critical thinking abilities, shorter attention spans, anxiety, and depression. While evidence connecting AI chatbots to suicide risk remains limited, several cases have prompted lawsuits alleging that interactions with chatbots contributed to young people’s deaths. Mr. Mamdani’s decision follows OpenAI’s launch of a teenage version of ChatGPT on August 18 featuring parental controls and content restrictions regarding self-harm and suicide. On August 26, Meta similarly announced stricter time limits, night-time blocking, and muted notifications during school hours for teenage accounts on Instagram and Facebook.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable but necessary. We do not see it that way,” Mr. Mamdani added.

Research supports a cautious stance. A 2026 CEPR discussion paper by researchers at Stockholm University and the University of Hong Kong examined more than 26,000 students in China over 30 months. They found that access to generative AI increased homework scores by 18% and reduced completion time by 30%. However, after roughly six months, the same students’ closed-book examination scores had fallen by 20%. A broader review by the Brookings Institution’s Centre for Universal Education, analysing over 400 studies and interviews with 500 educators and pupils across 50 countries, concluded that the potential harms of generative AI in primary and secondary education currently outweigh the benefits—though tailored applications with proper safeguards can enrich learning.

How are other parts of the world dealing with a similar dilemma? The United Arab Emirates is moving towards more structured AI education, rather than a moratorium. It has announced an AI curriculum across public and private schools covering areas such as data, algorithms, applications, risks and ethical use. It also plans to train about 22,000 educators in using AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis and lesson planning.

Norway has adopted a more cautious approach. Its education authorities have recommended that pupils in grades one to seven should not be given access to generative AI, while students in eight to 10 should be introduced to it gradually.

Australia has taken another route: a national framework for responsible and ethical use of generative AI in schools, rather than a blanket prohibition. The European Union, meanwhile, has sought to regulate high-risk uses of AI. Under the EU AI Act, certain systems used in education — including those involved in evaluating learning outcomes or determining access to education — can fall into the high-risk category. The legislation does not amount to a general ban on generative AI in schools.

Poland is going further in the opposite direction, investing almost 1.9 billion zloty to equip 12,000 schools with AI laboratory sets as part of its broader digital education push.

And where does India stand? India is closer to the integration camp. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 identifies artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies as important to India’s changing educational and employment landscape, and calls for contemporary subjects such as AI to be introduced at appropriate stages, alongside greater emphasis on computational thinking.

The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) introduced Artificial Intelligence as an optional sixth subject in Class IX from the 2019-20 academic session. More recently, for 2026-27, CBSE launched a dedicated Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence curriculum for Classes III to VIII, with AI and allied-subject curricula for Classes IX to XII also finalised. The curriculum emphasises logical reasoning, pattern recognition, algorithm design, data literacy and responsible and ethical AI use.

title: Industrial-Strength Natural Language Processing
description: spaCy is a free open-source library for Natural Language Processing in Python. It features NER, POS tagging, dependency parsing, word vectors and more.
fullText:
spaCy is designed to help you do real work — to build real products, or gather real insights. The library respects your time, and tries to avoid wasting it. It's easy to install, and its API is simple and productive.

spaCy excels at large-scale information extraction tasks. It's written from the ground up in carefully memory-managed Cython. If your application needs to process entire web dumps, spaCy is the library you want to be using.

Since its release in 2015, spaCy has become an industry standard with a huge ecosystem. Choose from a variety of plugins, integrate with your machine learning stack and build custom components and workflows.

spaCy v3.0 introduces a comprehensive and extensible system for configuring your training runs. Your configuration file will describe every detail of your training run, with no hidden defaults, making it easy to rerun your experiments and track changes. You can use the quickstart widget or the init config command to get started, or clone a project template for an end-to-end workflow.

spaCy's new project system gives you a smooth path from prototype to production. It lets you keep track of all those data transformation, preprocessing and training steps, so you can make sure your project is always ready to hand over for automation. It features source asset download, command execution, checksum verification, and caching with a variety of backends and integrations.

spaCy v3.0 introduces transformer-based pipelines that bring spaCy's accuracy right up to the current state-of-the-art. You can also use a CPU-optimized pipeline, which is less accurate but much cheaper to run.

title: Token Tap: extract design tokens from any webpage
description: Stop manually digging through devtools every time you inherit a site with no style guide.Token Tap is a Chrome extension that reads a webpage's actual rendered CSS and ranks every color, font, font size, border radius, and shadow by how often it's used — then lets you export the whole thing as clean JSON, CSS custom properties, or a ready-to-paste Tailwind config block.Who this is for: developers and designers reverse-engineering an undocumented site, agencies doing competitor or design audits, and anyone copying a reference site's look into Figma, Webflow, or Framer.What you get: the extension files plus a one-page install guide. It installs in under two minutes, no Chrome Web Store account needed.

title: From Shahed to Geran: How Russia Continues to Reinvent the One-Way Attack Drone
description: Since acquiring the original design from Iran, Russia has treated the Geran as a base platform for unprecedented wartime iteration. In a new brief, Kateryna Bondar and Nicole Errera trace the drone's evolution and draw lessons for U.S. policymakers.
fullText:
The defining challenge posed by Russia’s Geran program is the speed at which Russia can learn and adapt. Since acquiring the original Shahed design, Russia has treated the Geran as a continuously evolving platform, rapidly modifying its navigation, communications, payloads, propulsion, and tactics in response to changing Ukrainian defenses. Improvised modifications are tested in combat, successful solutions are standardized and scaled, and unsuccessful experiments are quickly discarded. This creates a continuous adaptation cycle in which battlefield feedback drives production decisions at a cadence measured in weeks rather than years. The Geran therefore illustrates a broader shift in modern weapons development: Advantage increasingly depends not on building the most advanced system at the outset, but on maintaining the organizational and industrial capacity to continuously iterate a system after it has entered combat. The central question is whether the United States is structured to compete with this model of rapid wartime adaptation.

The Shahed-class one-way attack drone has emerged as one of the defining assets of contemporary conflict. Originally developed by Iran and first deployed by Houthi insurgents against the Saudis in 2019, the system has since been replicated by a growing number of militaries and defense firms, including the United States, which deployed its Low-Cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System (LUCAS) for the first time in Operation Epic Fury, and China, which unveiled its Shahed copycat Feilong-300D at an air show in 2024. The Shahed’s expansive range, low cost, and high lethality against fixed targets have made its basic concept of a cheap, propellor-driven, delta-winged airframe carrying a substantial warhead over hundreds of miles a fixture of nearly every serious conversation about the future of strike warfare.

But the country that has most thoroughly mastered the Shahed is not the one that built it. Since acquiring the original design from Iran in 2022, Russia has used its license-built variant, designated the “Geran,” as a base platform for unprecedented wartime iteration. What distinguishes the Geran is not its technical sophistication, but how rapidly Russia has reconfigured the drone’s subsystems to adapt to changing battlefield conditions.

The Geran’s evolution over four years of combat in Ukraine offers one of the clearest views into what modern drone warfare looks like at the production level. It reflects rapid iteration cycles, parallel factories running competing design programs, integration of commercial off-the-shelf electronics from Chinese markets, and ad hoc modifications adopted as formal subsystems. More importantly, it reveals a model of wartime innovation built around speed, adaptation, and continuous feedback from the battlefield. This is a model that the United States is not currently structured to match, despite its efforts in the LUCAS program to replicate Russia’s success.

In mid-August 2022, roughly six months after launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia received its first shipment of Iranian-made Shahed-136 and Shahed-131 attack drones. The first publicly documented use of the Shahed-136 in Ukraine came a month later, when Ukrainian forces recovered the wreckage of a drone near Kupiansk on September 13. Although the drone was of Iranian origin, the recovered airframe was marked with the model name “Geran-2,” the Russian designation for the Shahed-136, and the series letter “M.” Later in 2023, Russian engineers introduced two more domestic variants marked “Ы” and “К.”

The Geran-M featured a delta airframe, 11.5 feet long with an 8.2-foot wingspan, made of fiberglass lined with carbon fiber and Nomex honeycomb—a heat-resistant composite that is both stiff and light. It carried a 50-horsepower piston engine produced by the Iranian company Oje Parvaz Mado Nafar Company (Mado), which has been sanctioned by both the United States and the European Union for providing engines for unmanned aerial vehicles to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (the engine itself is a reverse-engineered clone of the German Limbach L550E).

The M series was also equipped with a Nasir satellite receiver and a Sadra navigation unit, both of Iranian design, which combined global navigation satellite system (GNSS) capabilities with an inertial measurement unit to keep the system from straying too far from its preprogrammed route when the satellite signal was compromised. Its payload was a 118-pound two-stage penetrator warhead of Iranian origin, designed to punch through armor before detonating a main charge.

About two months after the Geran-M appeared in Ukraine, a delegation of Russian defense industry representatives traveled to Iran to finalize a $1.75 billion deal authorizing production of the drone on Russian soil—specifically, at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in the Republic of Tatarstan.

The Alabuga SEZ had been originally founded in 2006 with the goal of attracting investment from Western companies. But when those companies started pulling out of the region at the onset of the war in Ukraine, Alabuga pivoted to producing drones for Russia’s military. In the initial stages of the contract, Alabuga would receive components for assembly directly from Iran, making the first batch of Gerans to emerge from the facility virtually identical to the “M” variant with the exception of the letter “Ы” painted on the wingtips.

While Alabuga has become synonymous with production of the Geran, it is not Russia’s only domestic drone production facility. In 2023, JSC Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol, a subsidiary of state-owned defense firm Almaz-Antey, began operating a parallel production site in Izhevsk. The Kupol model, denoted by the letter “К” and also referred to as the Garpiya, saw several design modifications, mostly driven by Russia’s desire to reduce dependency on foreign components.

The Nomex honeycomb airframe lining was replaced with a thick foam layer sandwiched between what appears to be a carbon fiber–reinforced polymer coating. This kind of composite sandwich is used extensively in aerospace, valued for its strength and light weight, but similar polyurethane-foam structures have also been shown to mask radar signatures, a plausible explanation for the change.

The Iranian Mado engine was swapped for one of two Chinese copies of the same German Limbach design in a supply-chain hedge, while the Iranian Nasir satellite receiver was replaced with Russia’s Kometa-M4, integrated into a larger B-105 navigation module and moved inside the airframe. The original Iranian flight controller, comprising eight layers of circuit boards, was replaced with the Russian B-101, a four-layer design with 3D-printed supports and an integrated inertial measurement unit. The warhead shifted from the Iranian penetrator to the Russian BSF-50, a fragmentation-high-explosive design wrapped in tungsten balls for additional shrapnel.

The nature of the relationship between the two production sites, and whether they function more as competitors or collaborators, is not entirely clear. But when comparing the factories’ respective outputs—which would gradually expand beyond the variants Ы and К to include variants КБ, Ъ, КЦ, Э, and КК—two distinct development philosophies emerge.

Drones built in Izhevsk tend to be of higher production quality, while Alabuga models tend to be scrappier and strapped with ad hoc solutions to problems on the battlefield. In November 2023, for instance, Geran drones began appearing in black paint, allowing them to camouflage against the dark sky in night attacks. While К-series drones were painted uniformly, Ы models were initially only painted on their undersides, a half measure indicating the change had not yet been standardized.

That same month, a Geran-Ы drone was deployed with a 4G modem in a 3D-printed box taped to the outside of its tail fin along with two antennas and a portable power bank. This was not a formal modification—it was a hack, something built on a workbench, possibly by students at Alabuga Polytech, and taped onto a production drone before launch.

Over the years that followed, engineers at Alabuga would treat the Geran as a platform for innovation, testing new systems, serializing what worked and discarding what did not. Production would continue in parallel in Izhevsk. At times the sites would diverge, arriving at two different solutions to the same problem in the field. Other times they would converge on the same solution, indicating some level of coordination between the two programs.

The single clearest illustration of the Geran’s rapid development cycle is the progression of its satellite-navigation antennas to make it increasingly resilient to methods of electronic warfare (EW). EW involves jamming or spoofing GNSS signals to navigation systems and throwing unmanned systems off course. A Ukrainian Air Force official claimed in early 2026 that EW systems can neutralize nearly half the Geran drones launched in some night attacks.

Controlled reception pattern antenna (CRPA) technology is Russia’s best technical countermeasure against EW so far. Units such as the Kometa-M, Russia’s homegrown CRPA series, use several antenna elements to neutralize signal interference from multiple directions. EW resilience scales linearly with the number of elements: The four-element Kometa-M4 can resist three sources of interference, the eight-element Kometa-M8 can resist seven, and so on.

From 2023 to 2025, the number of antenna elements carried by the Geran grew exponentially. The original Iranian Nasir carried four antenna elements. The Nasir was swapped out for Russia’s Kometa-M4—another four-element unit—in mid-2023. Other Russian weapons systems were flying with the eight-element Kometa-R8 by March 2024. While it is unclear whether the Geran received the same upgrade, Ukraine’s monthly interception rate of Geran drones climbed from 77 percent in February 2024 to a high of 97 percent that May, and in what appears to be a Russian technical report on the Kometa-R8 published later that year (shared on Telegram by a Ukrainian analyst), the authors attribute the high interception rate to a flaw in the Kometa’s design. Where the original design apparently comprised two Kometa-M4 modules placed side by side, the authors of the report recommend an alternative configuration, with eight antenna elements arranged in a circle. A circular model was in use on the Geran by January 2025. And for the first time, the CRPA was a product not of Iran or Russia but of China.

This was the beginning of a spell of rapid-fire iteration. By March 2025, there was a 16-element version of the Chinese module, its antennas configured in two concentric rings. Another three months passed and a new Chinese variant emerged, this time with 16 antennas in a four-by-four array. Meanwhile, Gerans began to fly with the Kometa-M8 in addition to the new Kometa-M12, which featured 12 antenna elements in a three-by-four grid. By the end of 2025, Izhevsk drones were flying with the Kometa-M16—an unusual geometry of 16 patch antennas spread across three rows.

The plants at Izhevsk and Alabuga showed diverging supply chain preferences throughout this period, with the former leaning heavily on Russian Kometa modules and the latter importing units from China after exhausting its initial supply of Iranian Nasirs. But they still iterated at a similar cadence, suggesting that engineers at both sites were responding directly to improvements in Ukrainian EW.

The antenna counts trace the Ukrainian jamming curve. Every time Ukrainian EW got better at interfering with GPS signals, Russian and Chinese suppliers answered with more antenna elements and novel geometries. The cycle ran faster than any Western procurement program could plausibly match.

Ukraine’s anti-air defenses were not limited to EW tactics, and Russia’s attempts to thwart these defenses did not stop at CRPAs. While some Russian engineers were experimenting with increased antenna counts, others were trying out new ways of communicating with the drone mid-flight.

The earliest Gerans operated under fire-and-forget logic. They followed preprogrammed flight paths, relied on contested satellite signals to reach their targets, and had no way of communicating back to operators whether the mission had been a success.

The first attempt to establish communication between drone and operator came in November 2023, when the Geran carrying a 4G modem in a 3D-printed box taped to the outside of one winglet was found. Ukrainian analysts theorized that the module was intended to transmit the drone’s location over a Ukrainian cellular network mid-flight. If transmission cut out before the drone reached its target, Russian operators could infer the presence of anti-air defenses at the last transmitted location and program future Gerans to fly around the area. Several months later, another drone reportedly paired a 4G modem with a video camera attached to the top of the airframe, unlocking visual reconnaissance capabilities.

The success of these initial experiments was confirmed in early 2025. Ukrainian military intelligence shared that the Geran-2 series Ы and Ъ were flying with standardized telemetry modules. The formalized solution consisted of a Raspberry Pi minicomputer and two 3G/LTE modems produced by Chinese telecommunications firm ZTE. The modems carried both Russian and Ukrainian SIM cards for redundancy, a clear upgrade to the original design, which only contained a Ukrainian Kyivstar SIM card. By June 2025, almost all Gerans were flying with the new telemetry module taped outside the airframe, and by the end of that year, the unit seemed to have earned a place inside the body with the rest of the electronics. With that, the ad hoc solution had been incorporated into the drone’s design as a formal subsystem. The field experiment had become a production feature, still present in the Geran today.

Equally telling are the experimental systems that are seen once or twice before falling to the wayside. In September 2024, Ukrainian media reported a Geran-Ы had been downed with a Starlink terminal onboard. Like the modem that came before it, this appears to have been an experiment from Alabuga. Unlike the modem, Starlink did not become a serialized solution.

The Geran’s communication capabilities underwent another major shift in the summer of 2025, when Russians began equipping the drone with mesh radio network modems. The mesh radio XK-F358, produced by Chinese firm Xingkai Tech, transformed every drone that carried it into a signal repeater for other units nearby, forming an airborne network that facilitated not only the transmitting of information about air defenses and potential targets but also remote operator control in real time. Data could now be transmitted between an operator on the ground and a unit in the air via a “chain” of network nodes. If a link in the chain became compromised, the signal could dynamically reroute through another neighboring node, making the communication channel remarkably resilient (as long as there were enough nodes nearby). The effectiveness of the communication system was entirely dependent on the network’s density, making it difficult to deploy improvisationally. It tracks, then, that the modems were quickly scaled up. By early 2026, Gerans of all series were participants in the sprawling communication network, a testament to Russia’s ability to aggressively scale and synchronize across production sites when necessary.

The technical upgrade was accompanied by new tactics. Gerans were spotted flying in circles to act as radio repeaters and transmit control commands from operators in Russia deeper into Ukrainian territory.

Modems were also paired with a broad range of cameras, attached to the Geran in diverse configurations. Camera models ranged from cheap, off-the-shelf security cameras to the sophisticated Honpho TS130C-01 with long-wave infrared capabilities, a laser rangefinder covering up to two miles, and built-in computer vision. They were carried facing forward underneath the drone’s nose, sitting atop the nose and facing the rear, lodged inside the nose tip, and sticking up from a hole cut into the top of the nose. At least one version carried two cameras, one facing forward and the other backward; this model was armed with an air-to-air missile to take down interceptor drones and helicopters, and the positioning of the two cameras on the missile’s mount suggests a synthesis of innovation across component types.

With that, the Geran was no longer purely a preprogrammed munition flying to a fixed coordinate. It had become a remotely-piloted strike aircraft that could loiter, observe, identify targets, and be redirected mid-mission by an operator watching a live video feed—a fundamentally different weapon than the one that first appeared in Ukrainian skies in 2022.

As electronics grew more capable, the Geran’s payloads also grew heavier and more diverse.

The progression of the warhead was relatively straightforward. The original 118-pound Iranian penetrator gave way to the Russian 110-pound BSF-50 fragmentation warhead on the Geran-Ы and to the 115-pound BST-52 shaped-charge-incendiary on the К and КБ. By January 2025, two new 115-pound warheads had been introduced on the Ы—the OFZBCh-50 fragmentation-high-explosive-incendiary and the TBBCh-50M thermobaric, both of which were lined with metal balls for shrapnel. Before long, the Alabuga plant had expanded into nearly 200-pound explosives, arming the Ъ with the KOFZBCh-90 cumulative-fragmentation-high-explosive-incendiary unit. Izhevsk had a different approach, stacking two BST-52 warheads back-to-back in the fuselage for an almost 230-pound combined payload—a rare case of Izhevsk opting for an ad hoc solution while Alabuga took a more conventional route.

In 2025, Russia began experimenting with auxiliary munitions attached to the Geran for mid-flight release. Some, including the PTM-3 anti-tank mines carried under the wings, seemed intended to attack secondary targets en route to the final destination. Others, such as the R-60 air-to-air missile mounted on the drone’s fuselage, or the Verba man-portable air defense missile carried in addition to a primary warhead, were used to fend off anti-aircraft helicopters and interceptors. These new payloads spurred further improvisation: Within four months of the first R-60 on a Geran, drones were flying with decoy missiles to further complicate Ukrainian threat assessment. And in perhaps the most unusual case, in March 2026, a Geran was spotted carrying two first-person view drones on top of the airframe for mid-flight release. This highlights how even a technically primitive modification can radically transform the Geran’s role on the battlefield: With the addition of two drone mounts, the platform had become a drone mothership.

For most of the Geran’s life cycle, Russian engineers treated the drone as a chassis onto which new subsystems were hung without changing the structure of the chassis itself. All of the modifications described above, from novel payloads to increasingly EW-resistant satellite antennas, were implemented within and around the original Iranian airframe. This modular and incremental approach enabled Russia to achieve unprecedented wartime innovation. It allowed the drone’s subsystems to evolve in parallel and rapidly adapt to new battlefield conditions. But it also meant there was a ceiling for the performance gains any one modification could deliver.

This trade-off became particularly evident in Russia’s efforts to increase the Geran’s flight speed. As with many of the changes described above, the upgrade was motivated by increasingly effective Ukrainian anti-aircraft defenses. A faster Geran enabled by a turbojet engine could outrun interceptors and present a smaller window in which Ukrainian defenses could respond.

The first Geran to swap out its piston engine for a jet engine was of Iranian origin. Designated Shahed-238, this model was deployed in Ukraine as early as January 2024. It would be another year before Ukrainian military intelligence reported that Russia was setting up a domestic production line for the jet-powered Geran. This domestic variant, dubbed the Geran-3, was equipped with a Chinese Telefly JT80 turbojet engine that pushed it to speeds of up to 300 miles per hour—twice the maximum speed of the Geran-2.

However, the new model faced a critical limitation. It was flying with the same airframe as its piston-powered predecessor, and lacked the structural strength to withstand the G-load that came with such high speeds. Russia was running up against the ceiling of what it could achieve by swapping out individual components. To continue to innovate its way out of Ukrainian defenses, it would need to redesign the Iranian airframe. To scale production of the new model, it would have to upend its production lines.

That is exactly what it did. The result was the Geran-4 and Geran-5.

These models were introduced in 2026 and have many subsystems in common with the Geran-2 and Geran-3. Like the Geran-3, both fly with a Chinese Telefly turbojet engine (but a different model with greater thrust). Where they differ is the airframe. The Geran-4 features a more aerodynamic variant of the original delta shape, plus a reinforced structure that allows it to withstand significant G loads. It can maneuver at speeds of 186–249 miles per hour and achieve a maximum speed of 311 miles per hour. The Geran-5, on the other hand, eschews the delta-winged design entirely for a structure more typical of a cruise missile.

In August 2026, Ukrainian Defense Intelligence reported that Russia had halted production of its jet-powered Geran-3 kamikaze drones. It previously cut back on its attack drone production as it reoriented production lines around the two new models. In one sense, this is a break in a pattern. But it is also consistent with the doctrine of constant reinvention that Russia has followed with the Geran since 2023. Russian engineers will likely continue to innovate in modular, incremental fashion on top of the Geran-4—one base platform is simply getting swapped out for another.

These iterations reveal a fundamentally different model of weapons development—one that prioritizes speed, experimentation, and continuous adaptation over traditional, requirements-driven acquisition. There are three patterns that stand out.

First, new modifications are scrappy in the beginning and built around commercial components. Taped-on modules, 3D-printed parts, Chinese consumer electronics—all of these features are ways to iterate fast and not to be afraid of imperfection. Field experiments are encouraged and the most successful experiments are adopted and scaled rapidly, while less effective solutions are quickly discarded.

Second, iteration is driven by battlefield feedback rather than requirements documents. When Ukrainian jamming improved, antenna element counts went up. When interceptors began to pose a larger threat, the Geran got a jet engine to outrun them. Engineers did not set out to build the fastest or most EW-resilient system possible. They determined the minimum performance level needed to outmaneuver the enemy and delivered accordingly.

Third, the loop between what operators need and what engineers deliver is measured in weeks. Completed weapons move straight from production to the battlefield—one Geran shot down by Ukrainian forces on October 15, 2025, had its satellite receiver installed on October 8, meaning the unit was launched no more than one week after leaving the production line. There is no program office in that loop.

None of this is a tribute to Russian engineering brilliance. By most technical measures, the Geran drone is a crude weapon. Until 2026, its airframe remained unchanged from the original Iranian design. Its individual subsystems are, in isolation, unimpressive.

Russia’s achievement is not in any particular component, but in its approach to the underlying production and innovation model: two parallel factories competing on design, aggressive substitution of commercial off-the-shelf components, direct feedback from operators to engineers, permission for factory-floor modifications without lengthy requalification and certifications, and acceptance that a meaningful fraction of fielded units will be experimental.

Each of those practices runs into a specific constraint in the United States. U.S. programs of record are structured around single primes rather than competing production lines on the same platform. U.S. qualification standards treat integration of commercial components as a risk to be managed, not a normal engineering practice. U.S. acquisition rules treat fielded systems as finished products whose modifications require formal engineering change proposals. None of these features are accidents, and most of them exist for defensible reasons. But the combined effect is that U.S. manufacturers cannot iterate on a deployed strike drone at a cadence measured in days or weeks.

Kateryna Bondar is a senior fellow with the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington, D.C. Nicole Errera is a research assistant for the Wadhwani AI Center at CSIS.

title: These Cyborg Cockroaches Could Save Your Life
description: The team embedded electrodes into live cockroaches, then outfitted them with cameras and injection devices to deliver medication via remote control.
fullText:
drones have increasingly been used to help respond to disasters, reaching locations that are too hard or too dangerous to send humans, such as collapsed buildings. Many of these efforts have been focused on search and rescue. But new research shows how bugs—with their ability to crawl through even narrower gaps in rubbled—outfitted with electrodes could be used as the next generation of first responders.

A research team from the University of Queensland (UQ) and the University of New South Wales (UNSW) have developed the “Paraborg” to not only help with searching for victims, but also administer first aid. While the idea of receiving medical care from a cockroach might be a little skin-crawling, the new cyborg bug could one day help buy human rescuers valuable time in a disaster zone.

“Cyborg insects have been designed for ‘search and explore’ missions for the past couple of decades,” Tan Vo Doan, a bio-robotics researcher at UQ, says in a press release. “We wanted to take the next step.”

The team relied on a giant burrowing cockroach that inhabits northern Queensland to develop the Paraborg, which they documented in a recent paper published the journal Advanced Science. The armored cockroach is up to 87 millimeters (3.5 inches) in length and weighs up to 40 grams (1.4 ounces).

Taking advantage of this large size, the research team developed two types of Paraborgs with different functions: one equipped with a camera to film the condition of disaster victims, and another with an automatic injection mechanism to administer medication. Cockroaches can carry up to 1.5 times its body weight. In practice, a cockroach equipped with the injection mechanism saw its total height increase by about 15 millimeters and its weight by about 17 grams, which the study found did not significantly impair its normal movements. To create the cyborg cockroaches, the team anesthetized them when the electrodes and microchips were attached, and they lived as normal cockroaches once the equipment was removed.

They were able to steer the roach by stimulating each antenna independently, while stimulating both cerci controlled the pace. The scientists administered different frequencies between 10 and 40 hertz after finding that anything over 50 hertz became ineffective over time.

title: Local 3D LLM Sandbox a tiny assistant with an attitude
description: Talk to a tiny sassy robot and she builds your voxel world. Fully local: Gemma 4 + Whisper + Supertonic. - franciscocarloserra/llm-sandbox
fullText:
Meet a tiny robot with a big attitude. Hold a button, tell her "build me a tower", and she does: blind, never seen a thing, absolutely sure she just made a masterpiece. Wrong height, wrong place, zero doubt, plenty of sass. She lives entirely on your own machine: local model, local ears, local voice, no cloud. Come argue with her.

This is not a game. It is a test of one idea: split the controls by how fast your intent is.

Everything else follows from that split. The character talks back right away so the wait feels like a conversation, not a loading bar. A ghost outline appears where you aimed the instant you release the button, before the model has said a word. And the model is blind on purpose: it never sees the world, only what you point at and what you say. The gap between what you asked and what she proudly delivers is where the fun lives. We tried to fix it and the game got worse.

All local, all open weights, one consumer GPU (tested on an RTX 3090).

The model does not emit cubes. It emits volumes with stretch labels ("tall", "flat", "wide"), which the client expands into blocks. Same token budget, objects ten times bigger. Two model calls run per turn against a single llama.cpp slot: a tiny one for the spoken acknowledgement, a bigger one for the build. The small one hides most of the latency of the big one.

Every number lives in config.js. Voice pitch, ghost size, token budgets, detail levels, language markers, key bindings. If you want her sillier, faster or bigger, change a number. You never have to read the logic.

You need Python 3, a browser (Firefox or Chrome), a GPU that fits a ~15 GB GGUF, and three local services. They are not part of this repo; anything that speaks the same contract works.

The llama-server command we run:

Override anything with env vars: SANDBOX_PORT, STT_URL, TTS_URL, LLM_URL, LOCAL_TOKEN.

Click the page, hold right click, talk.

MIT. audio/Level_One_Morning.mp3 is the only bundled asset; see its own license.
